articles.title: World Matchplay Darts: James Wade battles through on 21st appearance in Blackpool as Gian van Veen comes up with crucial victory
articles.summary: James Wade, Gian van Veen, Michael van Gerwen, and Gary Anderson were among the players to pick up wins on Sunday; you can watch the World Matchplay live on Sky Sports in Blackpool until July 26
articles.body:
​​​​​2007 World Matchplay champion Wade is looking to finally clinch the Phil Taylor trophy once again after finishing runner-up in this tournament on six occasions in 2006, 2008, 2011, 2012, 2015 and 2025.

On his 21st Matchplay appearance, Wade had the early advantage as he took four legs on the spin in the first session to take a comprehensive 4-1 lead, Wattimena's levels sub-par for the TV stage.

The Dutchman came through with a flurry of strong legs and two breaks of throw which helped him battle back to 5-4.

Despite the resurgence, Wade capitalised when Wattimena's level faded away for a second time, allowing 'The Machine' to take out three legs in a row for an 8-4 advantage.

It was then a tense few legs as breaks of throw were traded, Wade eventually clinching tops for the win in Blackpool.

Wade was, as ever, honest in his assessment of his own performance, declaring that he was "rubbish".

"I was really, really lucky. I didn't do what I normally do," Wade told Sky Sports .

"I slowed him down, not purposely, but he pushes and pushes, as he has done the last four games between us.

"I slowed myself down and walked around rather than speeding up.

"In the end, the proof was in the pudding.

"It's hard to process. I normally go so fast playing Wattimena, and this time I thought: 'I'm going to do what I want to do, not what you want me to do.'"

He will face Ryan Searle who came through with a 10-6 win over William O'Connor.

O'Connor, who was on his Matchplay debut, was put to the sword by Searle early on as some clinical doubling and two breaks of throw had him 6-1 in the lead in no time.

The Irishman did battle back to bring the game to 8-6 but it was not enough as Searle found his trebles once again to secure the result, taking it out on tops.

Van Veen finds confidence boosting win as Nijman brings floor form to stage

Gian van Veen showed some incredible finishing in a 10-6 win over Krzysztof Ratajski in what was a confidence boosting win for the world No 3.

Ratajski had beaten Van Veen less than a week ago on the way to winning his third Euro Tour title in Leverkusen but Van Veen showed why he is one of the world's best in Blackpool, especially on the outer ring.

Two early 144 checkouts set the precedent and a huge 160 checkout in the 13th leg for a break of throw set the Winter Gardens alight.

The 'Polish Eagle' did keep coming throughout the contest, but was always kept at least three legs away from Van Veen as he just defended his own throw incredibly well.

"Everyone knows I have been struggling the last few months, and I just needed that win today," Van Veen told Sky Sports .

"My finishing got me through that game today.

"I am finishing really well, my scoring needs to be up there the next round.

"It is very important to have a good run. I have been up and down.

"To go deep here would mean so much confidence for myself going into the back end of this year."

He faces Wessel Nijman after the Dutchman showed why he has been the player to beat in 2026 with a comprehensive 10-5 win against Dave Chisnall.

Nijman has won eight titles in 2026, but the Matchplay marked the tournament at which it was time to convert his floor form into a big stage performance.

That he did when he picked up the first four legs and got as far as 6-1 in front. Chisnall did manage to pick up a few legs on the way but after nullifying 'Chizzy's' break of throw, Nijman held his throw all the way to a brilliant 108 checkout for victory.

Michael van Gerwen ground out a nervous win over Andrew Gilding, while Gary Anderson delivered his best-ever World Matchplay performance on Sunday afternoon in Blackpool.

Van Gerwen, who narrowly missed D12 for a nine-darter in the sixth leg, averaged less than 95 in a 10-6 victory over the dogged Gilding who refused to surrender the lead in the first half of their round one contest.

Earlier, former world champion Anderson delivered the best performance of the tournament so far in a 10-2 thrashing of Ryan Joyce.

The Scotsman averaged just under 110 - his best in 18 years of playing at the Winter Gardens - and delivered spectacular finishes of 144 and 141 to win.

He will take on Jonny Clayton in the next round, who rounded out the afternoon session with a 10-7 win over Damon Heta, holding off a fight back from 'The Heat' with a 121 finish on the bullseye then a 144 finish to win the contest Clayton's stand out moments.

In the first game of the day, the 13th seed Chris Dobey missed four match darts before losing 13-11 to Dirk van Duijvenbode , Dobey paying for missing 29 doubles in the game.

What's happening at the World Matchplay on Monday?

The first round of the World Matchplay Darts continues on Monday with four more big games coming your way, live on Sky Sports from 7pm.

Ross Smith opens the show against Kevin Doets , as Gerwyn Price then starts his Matchplay campaign against German No 1 Martin Schindler .

2024 Matchplay champion and World No 2 Luke Humphries headlines the evening with a mouth-watering clash against Cameron Menzies .

Danny Noppert then rounds out the evening when he takes on 'Voltage' Rob Cross.

Who will win this year's World Matchplay Darts? Luke Littler will be defending his title and you can watch all the action on Sky Sports. Stream darts and more top sport with NOW .

articles.title: World Matchplay Darts: Cameron Menzies dubs Luke Humphries win 'biggest moment of career' eight months after hand surgery
articles.summary: Cameron Menzies reflects on the 'biggest moment of [his] career' after his 10-7 win over World No 2 Luke Humphries; you can watch the World Matchplay live on Sky Sports in Blackpool until July 26
articles.body:
Menzies pulled out an incredible Big Fish checkout to beat world No 2 Humphries 10-7 in his first-ever triumph at Winter Gardens.

The monumental victory was a full-circle moment for the Scot, and represents a remarkable turnaround in fortune just eight months after he required surgery for punching a table during his first-round defeat to Josh Manby at the World Championship.

"I don't know how to explain that [victory]. I did believe in my heart that I could maybe cause an upset but I would have to play it out of my skin," Menzies said.

"I wouldn't say I played it out of my skin, but I played really well. I did say before the game started, to beat Luke, I need to take every chance that he gives me.

"It's not like Luke to give a lot of chances away but obviously I'm going to take it. A lot went in. I was happy. I stole a few legs to win but it's made the best moment of my darts career."

The Scot revealed in February that he considered giving up darts altogether , but reflected on his greatest ever win after a "terrible" start to 2026, which also included the death of his uncle:

"It's up there because I didn't think I was going to qualify for this.

"The start of the year, I was terrible. I was just really bad. I had a really poor start to the year but I went through a lot.

"I'm in a better place mentally and physically. I'm enjoying darts again."

Mardle: Menzies knows he can handle anything now

"It's his best ever win, and he mentioned that.

"With Cameron Menzies, everyone mentions his emotions, but it's the way he had to win that game.

"Nothing went according to plan. He was broken back early twice, that's up and down emotions. The high of breaking to being broken back.

"Then he went on a run, and got pegged back.

"There was a lot happening in that game, but he held it all together beautifully.

"Humphries had an amazing spell of four legs, but then Menzies found a level again, and that's something we don't see enough.

"What he should take away from tonight was the way he handled this situation. It was like he was there a million times before.

What is happening on Wednesday at the World Matchplay?

The round two action continues on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports, with four more big matches coming your way.

Cameron Menzies will be looking to back up a huge win over world No 2 Luke Humphries when he takes on Ross Smith.

Gerwyn Price then takes on fellow former world champion Rob Cross.

World No 3 Gian van Veen faces a showdown against fellow Dutchman and in-form Wessel Nijman, with James Wade taking on Ryan Searle.

articles.title: Probamos el GAC Aion UT: el SUV eléctrico chino con modo antimareo
articles.standfirst: La marca china ligada a Toyota lanza en España su segundo modelo, un SUV eléctrico compacto con 201 CV que parte de los 22.945 euros (con ayudas y descuentos).
articles.summary: La marca china ligada a Toyota lanza en España su segundo modelo, un SUV eléctrico compacto con 201 CV que parte de los 22.945 euros (con ayudas y descuentos).
articles.body: Una de las marcas orientales de más reciente introducción en el mercado español es GAC. Sin embargo, en China tiene un gran peso específico y una larga asociación de veinte años con Toyota, que acaba de incrementarse recientemente: su bZ3X lleva motor GAC y los próximos modelos de la marca china contarán con propulsores híbridos de Toyota. Además, GAC ha implantado una fábrica y un departamento de diseño en Europa. El equipo de diseño encargado del Aion UT tiene su sede en Milán y su director es francés. Y, para el montaje de los coches en suelo europeo, se ha recurrido a la fábrica de Steyr en Graz (Austria). Eso demuestra el interés y la planificación de la firma china para encajar a la perfección en el mercado del Antiguo Continente. En España ofrece ya dos modelos de Aion (el V y el UT) y ya ha abierto treinta concesionarios por su geografía. El nuevo Aion UT es un SUV compacto de 4,27 metros de longitud y una amplia distancia entre ejes de 2,75. Para los diseñadores de GAC el exterior no lo es todo: tenía mucha importancia la habitabilidad interior y el confort de los ocupantes (hasta 5, aunque 4 viajan mucho mejor). Y ofrece un gran maletero de entre 440 y 1.600 litros de capacidad. El Aion UT parte de la plataforma AEP 5.0 y cuenta con una batería de LFP diseñada y fabricada por la propia GAC. Es de formato sándwich, refrigerada por líquido y muy compacta. Tiene una capacidad de 60 kWh, que le aportan una autonomía WLTP de 430 km (más en ciclo urbano). El motor eléctrico delantero síncrono produce 150 kW (201 CV) y es muy compacto, acelerando de 0 a 100 km/h en 7,3 segundos. La carrocería diseñada en Italia tiene su propia personalidad, especialmente gracias al gran parabrisas delantero, muy largo e inclinado, que reduce la superficie del capó delantero. El morro cuenta con una parrilla muy baja para refrigerar el radiador de la batería y el motor. También dispone de bomba de calor de muy bajo consumo, una de las aportaciones tecnológicas avanzadas de GAC. Efectivamente, el habitáculo ha sido muy pensado y rezuma estilo europeo. Especialmente luminoso es el acabado Luxury con tapizado en simil cuero blanco (también puede contar con techo solar panorámico). Los asientos delanteros son muy envolventes, están calefactados (y refrigerado el del conductor) y los respaldos pueden reclinarse 180º y unirse a la banqueta trasera para una buena siesta. Los asientos traseros cuentan con un amplio espacio para las piernas y un suelo muy bajo. Bajando el reposabrazos, los pasajeros van tan cómodos como los de delante. El GAC Aion UT ha superado con 5 estrellas las pruebas de colisión Euro NCAP y dispone de grandes airbags de cortinilla, además de una gran resistencia estructural (el techo de cristal soporta hasta 7 toneladas). Pero además goza de un completo paquete de ADAS, de cámara 360º en 3D y de conducción autónoma de nivel 2. El conductor dispone de un cuadro de información completo (aunque con grafía muy pequeña) y de una gran pantalla de 14,6” con todos los demás comandos. Una vez más criticamos esa moda china de meter en la pantalla desde el reglaje de los retrovisores a la apertura de la cortina del techo, pasando por los niveles de retención de frenada, dirección asistida, etc, etc. Cuando se intenta que el conductor no pierda atención al tráfico, se le obliga a navegar por menús y sub-menús para hacer ajustes necesarios… Al menos las alarmas interiores de las ADAS no son muy ruidosas, aunque mantenimiento de carril o de distancia son bastante intrusivas y sorprenden. Al volante, el Aion UT se comporta perfectamente. Es bastante silencioso, acelera con presteza y tiene una suspensión confortable. Incluso lleva un botón “antimareo” para suavizar las aceleraciones y retenciones lineales (no laterales). Hay tres niveles de retención que se combinan con los tres modos de conducción, pero ninguno resulta tan violento como para marear a nadie… No llega a tener “e-pedal”, aunque tiene una clara vocación urbana. Su tecnología se complementa con un app para el móvil con multitud de funciones remotas y el confort interior con hasta 24 espacios porta-objetos. GAC garantiza el Aion UT por 8 años o 160.000 km y la batería por 8 años o 200.000 km. Se comercializa en dos acabados: Premium y Luxury (con distinto equipamiento) y en seis colores diferentes de carrocería. La lista de precios antes de ayudas y descuentos oscila entre 34.495 y 39.495 euros. Pero, aprovechando la financiación de la marca y los descuentos y ayudas oficiales, los precios pueden llegar a 22.945 o 24.945 euros (Premium y Luxury). Tras estos dos modelos eléctricos, GAC se apresta a lanzar en el mercado europeo híbridos enchufables.

articles.title: Nolan Wells murder case update: Forensic expert clarifies what happened to deleted Snapchat messages
articles.summary: The mystery surrounding Nolan Wells’ phone has taken another turn after a digital forensic expert hired by the teenager’s family clarified what he meant
articles.body: The mystery surrounding Nolan Wells’ phone has taken another turn after a digital forensic expert hired by the teenager’s family clarified what he meant when he previously discussed deleted messages. Andrew Garrett said Snapchat messages had been remotely recalled or deleted by their senders, but he found no evidence that someone unlocked and tampered with Wells’ phone after his disappearance. The distinction is significant because it separates deleted Snapchat content from claims that someone accessed Wells’ device.Nolan Wells phone records offer a clearer pictureGarrett addressed the issue during a livestream published on YouTube on September 27. He explained that messages exchanged through Snapchat can be removed remotely by the person who sent them.“When we say erased from the phone, you’ve got to be a little careful with that. What happens is, when you and I are in conversation on Snapchat, and you decide to delete the messages on my side of the phone, you can do that remotely. That was done. There are some messages that were recalled and deleted from the phone,” Garrett said.He then stressed that his findings should not be interpreted as proof that someone physically accessed Wells’ device.“I didn’t say somebody unlocked the phone and started playing with the phone and started deleting the phone because that’s exactly what I would’ve said,” he added.Garrett said his examination also identified interactions with the device, such as the screen being activated, but those actions did not show that someone had unlocked it.Deleted Snapchat messages draw fresh attentionAlmost 3,000 Snapchat records from Wells’ account were released by Garrett’s forensic company. The records include group conversations in which people began raising concerns about Wells’ whereabouts on July 5.Some messages had disappeared, but the available evidence indicated they were deleted by the senders rather than by someone operating Wells’ account or phone. Garrett said Wells’ phone was last used at about 2:17 or 2:18 p.m. on July 4 and remained locked until it reached his family on July 5.The distinction has also become part of a dispute between Wells’ family and attorneys for three friends who were with him before his death. Those attorneys deny that their clients deleted messages from Wells’ phone and have disputed claims attributed to the family’s forensic examiner.Their representatives have also said they intend to sue family attorney Ben Crump for defamation.The forensic clarification does not resolve the wider questions surrounding Wells’ disappearance and death. Instead, it narrows one specific issue: deleted Snapchat messages do not, based on Garrett’s explanation, establish that someone gained access to Wells’ locked phone.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: "You carry it with you": Justine Pissott breaks her silence with heartbreaking sexual assault revelation amid Cornell 7 case
articles.summary: Justine Pissott has spoken publicly about surviving sexual assault, explaining why the continuing attention around the Cornell 7 case has been especially
articles.body: Justine Pissott has spoken publicly about surviving sexual assault, explaining why the continuing attention around the Cornell 7 case has been especially difficult for her. The Las Vegas Aces guard shared the deeply personal message on Instagram as public discussion intensified around allegations involving seven former Cornell University fraternity members. Rather than focusing only on the allegations, Pissott used her platform to highlight the lasting impact trauma can have on survivors and the importance of offering compassion instead of questioning how they respond.Justine Pissott shares personal sexual assault experiencePissott, 22, said the Cornell case brought back emotions connected to her own experience. In a message shared on September 29, she explained that she had rarely spoken about what happened to her but felt compelled to do so after seeing the public reaction to the case.“This is a vulnerable message but something I want to share,” Pissott began. “As someone who has been drugged and rap--, the Cornell 7 situation has been really hard for me to see. It hits a place in me that I don’t talk about often.”She went on to describe how the effects of sexual assault can continue long after the incident itself.“When something like this happens to you, it doesn’t just end when that night ends. You carry it with you. The confusion, the pieces you can’t remember, questioning yourself, blaming yourself, and trying to understand how someone could take advantage of you when you weren’t even able to protect yourself.”Pissott also addressed the scrutiny survivors can face when they choose to speak about their experiences.Cornell 7 case sparks wider conversation about survivorsThe basketball player said people often ask why survivors waited to speak, remained silent or behaved differently afterwards. She argued that trauma does not follow one predictable pattern.She also expressed support for the woman at the centre of the Cornell case and said survivors should not feel pressured to respond in a particular way.Pissott said she was not sharing her story to receive sympathy. Instead, she wanted other survivors to know they were not alone.“And if sharing even a small part of my story makes another survivor feel less alone, then it’s worth it,” Pissott wrote.She ended by offering encouragement to survivors and calling for an environment where people can speak about sexual assault without being judged for how they coped with the experience.The Cornell case involves a civil complaint filed by a former student against Cornell University and seven Chi Phi fraternity members. The allegations remain allegations, and the defendants’ legal responses are part of the ongoing proceedings.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Ricky Hatton’s £30m estate: Son Campbell says family is ‘completely in the dark’ as questions grow over the late boxer’s finances
articles.summary: Ricky Hatton’s family is still waiting for clarity over the former boxing champion’s finances, more than a year after his death.
articles.body: Ricky Hatton’s family is still waiting for clarity over the former boxing champion’s finances, more than a year after his death. New figures suggest Hatton left an estate worth around £30 million, built through his boxing career, businesses and property investments. But his son Campbell Hatton says the family has had little information about what happened to the money. Campbell told The Sun: “My family is still completely in the dark. We’ve had no involvement in my dad’s finances for over 15 years.” Trustees were appointed to handle the estate, but questions over its distribution remain.Ricky Hatton’s £30m estate and business assetsHatton, who died aged 46 in September 2025, built much of his wealth during a successful boxing career. He later put money into businesses and property, with the latest figures putting the value of his business interests at more than £20 million and property investments at around £10 million. These figures are estimates based on company accounts and reported property holdings, rather than a confirmed amount that his children will receive.Companies House records showed around 20 businesses linked to Hatton when he died. One of them, DHT Finance Limited, was valued at more than £18 million, while CWR 2021 Limited was worth almost £2.5 million. Some businesses, however, had liabilities. RHHP Limited was reported to have net liabilities of more than £2.1 million.Hatton was also linked to property investments, including a significant stake in a Leicester development valued at about £30 million. That figure refers to the development itself and should not be treated as Hatton’s personal wealth.The family’s uncertainty is linked in part to the absence of a will. Trustees were appointed to deal with the estate, but reports say communication between them and people close to Hatton’s family has become difficult. The Sun reported that one source described the situation as a “complete mess”.Hatton was understood to have wanted his wealth to provide for his three children, Campbell, 25, and daughters Millie and Fearne. However, there is still no clear public timetable for when or how the estate will be distributed.Ricky Hatton’s £1.5m house sold after his deathAnother part of Hatton’s property holdings was his home in Gee Cross, Greater Manchester. The five-bedroom house was eventually sold for £1.5 million this year, after initially being listed for £1.85 million. The property was taken off the market after Hatton’s death and later returned with lower asking prices before the sale. The Daily Mail previously reported the £1.5 million sale, citing Land Registry records.The sale is separate from the wider £30 million estimate and does not by itself show how much money will eventually pass to Hatton’s children.For Campbell, the main issue is still knowing what his father left behind and what will happen to it. The latest reports have brought more figures into the public domain, but the family is still waiting for clearer answers about the estate.Ricky Hatton’s estate is estimated at around £30 million, with more than £20 million linked to businesses and another £10 million in property investments.His son Campbell says the family is still “completely in the dark” about the finances. articles.summary: Magnus Carlsen, widely regarded as one of the greatest chess players ever, recently suffered a surprise defeat in a blitz game against Bulgarian chess
articles.body: Magnus Carlsen, widely regarded as one of the greatest chess players ever, recently suffered a surprise defeat in a blitz game against Bulgarian chess creator Volen Dyulgerov, better known online as Witty Alien or the "shirtless guy" these days.The upset happened on September 30 during Chess.com’s first Chess Club Showdown.Who is Witty Alien?Dyulgerov, born in 1999, is a Candidate Master (CM) from Bulgaria. His highest FIDE rating was 2200, reached in 2023, while his rating stood at 2181 in September 2026.Although he is a decent over-the-board player, he has become much more popular through online chess and content creation.Known for his energetic personality, Witty Alien has built a following on YouTube and online chess platforms.Chess.com named him Creator of the Month in July 2024 and credited him with the popular Alien Gambit.His Chess.com blitz rating is around 2612, while Carlsen’s is about 3396, making the victory even more unexpected. Magnus Carlsen was visibly stunnedThe game, which ended in the five-time world champion visibly looking stunned after the defeat to the Bulgarian, was part of the Chess Club Showdown, a two-hour five-minute blitz event featuring nine chess clubs.Amateur players had the chance to face major stars such as Carlsen, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Anish Giri.Carlsen represented Team Liquid Chess Club, which finished second in the main arena with 2312 points. 9z Globant topped the standings with 2368 points and later won the final 53.5-45.5.Also Read: ‘Sometimes in chess, there are just these blind spots’: Nihal Sarin looks back at his Chess Olympiad loss to Uzbekistan | ExclusiveCarlsen managed to win both of his games on board one during the final, but he had already suffered a defeat earlier in the event. articles.title: Former WWE US Champion "took a paycut" to re-sign with the company
articles.summary: A former WWE United States Champion had a lengthy stint in WWE before being released in 2016.
articles.body: A former WWE United States Champion had a lengthy stint in WWE before being released in 2016. He returned to the company a decade later after a spectacular run on the independent circuit. The star is Matt Cardona. He returned to the Stamford-based wrestling promotion this year and made a major revelation about his return to WWE.Matt Cardona took a pay cut to re-sign with WWEIn an interview with Jeremy Jacobowitz, Matt Cardona revealed that he made more money outside WWE. In a surprise turn of events, the former WWE Tag Team Champion decided to take a pay cut to rejoin the company. Cardona did so as he called being in WWE the ultimate opportunity if it worked out, so he decided to take that risk.Cardona said, "I made more money outside WWE than I ever made in WWE. Like, I technically took a pay cut to go back to WWE. You know what I’m saying? That’s how much money I was making on the indies. But WWE, going back, is the ultimate opportunity.‘Cause if it works out, it’ll be the ultimate raise, right?Like, I’m sitting here talking to you because WWE set this up."What was Matt Cardona's mindset after being released by WWE?In the same interview, Cardona reflected on the three paths he had after being released by WWE. He chose the path Honky Tonk Man took after his WWE stint ended. At the same time, he wanted to reinvent himself and not be 'Zack Ryder' on the indies. Instead, he became his authentic self, Matt Cardona, which was one of the biggest names on the independent circuit."I knew then I had three options because I’m a student of the game. I see what happens when people leave WWE. You can fade into obscurity, right, which I wasn’t going to do. You can, you know, just be bitter and negative, fade into obscurity. Or you can, like, just coast off your WWE name forever.I don’t mean, like, the literal name. Like, Honky Tonk Man is still doing the Shake, Rattle and Roll and the jump, and I love that, and it’s great. I love Honky. But I didn’t want to still do the ‘woo woo woo’ on the indies", said Cardona.A major advantage for Cardona that came from signing with WWE was that he was able to work and travel with his real-life wife, Chelsea Green. The couple are currently a part of SmackDown, where Green is the reigning WWE Women's Champion and was even featured in an in-ring altercation with Gunther. Shooting and boxing followed with three gold medals each, while wrestling contributed two.India also won two gold medals apiece in cricket, hockey and kabaddi, with both men's and women's teams contributing to the country's strong finish.85 medals across 21 sportsIndia's medals came across 21 sports, demonstrating the breadth of its performance at the continental event.Alongside the major medal-winning disciplines, India also secured podium finishes in weightlifting, wushu, badminton, kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and table tennis.The 85-medal haul was India's second-highest ever at the Asian Games, behind the record 106 medals won at Hangzhou 2023.India's final tally of 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals secured the country a fourth-place finish in the overall medal standings.Athletics leads India’s medal chargeAthletics was the backbone of India's medal campaign, producing a wide range of podium finishes across track and field events.India won gold in the women's 4x400m relay, while athletes also collected medals in the 10,000m, 1500m, marathon, shot put, long jump, high jump, javelin throw, pole vault, 400m hurdles, 5000m, 3000m steeplechase, 200m, decathlon and relay events.Gulveer Singh was among India's standout performers, winning silver in the men's 10,000m and 1500m events and bronze in the 5000m.Sawan Berwal won silver in the men's marathon, becoming India's first marathon medallist at the Asian Games since 1982 while also setting a national record.Sarvesh Kushare ended India's 56-year wait for a men's high jump medal, while Baranica Elangovan created history by becoming the first Indian pole vaulter to win an Asian Games medal.Vithya Ramraj added another landmark performance by winning bronze in the women's 400m hurdles and breaking a national record that had stood for 42 years.Shooting delivers 15 medalsShooting once again played a major role in India's Asian Games campaign, contributing 15 medals, including three golds.Neeru Dhanda won India's first individual gold medal of the Games in the women's trap competition. She later combined with Kynan Chenai to win gold in the mixed trap event.Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh also won gold in the mixed team 10m air pistol event, matching the Asian record.India's shooters also collected medals in the 10m air rifle, 50m rifle 3P, 25m pistol, trap and skeet events.Archery produces five gold medalsArchery was India's most successful sport in terms of gold medals, with five titles.Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Prithika Pradeep and Chikitha Taniparthi won gold in the women's compound team event, while Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Jadhav claimed the mixed compound team title.Sahil Jadhav, Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru and Kushal Dalal won the men's compound team gold.The women's recurve team of Ankita Bhakat, Kumkum Mohod and Kirti Sharma also finished on top.Kumkum then produced one of the defining moments of the Games by winning India's first-ever women's individual recurve gold medal at the Asian Games.Boxing delivers three gold medalsIndia enjoyed a strong showing in boxing, winning three gold medals.Lovlina Borgohain became only the second Indian woman to win an Asian Games boxing gold, following Mary Kom's historic achievement at the 2014 Incheon Games.Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also won gold medals in their respective categories.India added bronze medals through Narender Berwal, Priya Ghanghas and Kapil Pokhariya.Wrestling adds two gold medalsIndia's wrestlers also made their mark in Aichi-Nagoya.Aman Sehrawat won gold in the men's 57kg category, while Sujeet Kalkal became champion in the men's 65kg event.Nitesh Kumar and Antim Panghal won silver medals, while Sunil Kumar and Deepak Punia added bronze medals.Cricket and hockey provide golden finishIndia's team sports produced a spectacular late surge.The men's and women's cricket teams successfully defended their Asian Games titles. The men's team defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final, while the women's team beat Sri Lanka to retain the gold medal.Hockey also delivered two gold medals.The Indian women's hockey team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games title, while the men's team, led by Harmanpreet Singh, completed its campaign with a commanding 5-1 victory over Malaysia in the final.The men's hockey gold was India's 21st gold medal of the Games and sealed the country's fourth-place finish.Historic gold for Pranavi UrsGolf produced another landmark moment for India.Pranavi Urs won the women's individual gold medal, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games gold in golf.India also won silver in the women's team event through Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar.Mirabai Chanu wins first Asian Games medalOlympic medallist Mirabai Chanu claimed silver in the women's 49kg weightlifting event.It was her first Asian Games medal and ended India's wait for a medal in the sport since the 1998 Bangkok Games.Wushu athlete Roshibina Devi also continued her impressive continental run by winning her third consecutive Asian Games medal, taking silver in the women's 60kg sanda event.Squash stars add to India’s medal haulIndia's squash contingent also delivered multiple podium finishes.Abhay Singh and Anahat Singh won silver in the men's and women's singles events respectively.Anahat's silver made her the first Indian woman to win a singles silver medal in squash at the Asian Games.India also won bronze medals in mixed doubles and the men's and women's team events.Several firsts for IndiaThe Aichi-Nagoya campaign was notable not just for the medal count but also for the number of historic achievements.Kumkum Mohod became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold.Suchika Tariyal secured India's first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts, while Jay Meena became the country's first Asian Games medallist in soft tennis after reaching the men's singles semifinals.India also ended long medal droughts in several athletics disciplines.Olympic qualification adds another dimensionIndia's success in Aichi-Nagoya also carried significance for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.India secured Olympic quotas through its performances in archery and hockey. The Asian Games offered Olympic qualification opportunities in seven sports — archery, hockey, sailing, squash, surfing, tennis and triathlon.India secured places in both men's and women's hockey as well as in archery's compound mixed team and women's individual recurve events.India fall short of Hangzhou record but finish stronglyIndia's 85-medal haul was 21 medals fewer than its record 106 at Hangzhou, while the gold-medal count dropped from 28 to 21.However, the final standings did not tell the entire story of India's campaign.As recently as Thursday, India had only 10 gold medals and was outside the top 10 of the medal table. A remarkable late surge changed the complexion of the campaign.India won 12 medals on Friday, including six golds, before adding nine medals on the penultimate day. Gold medals in cricket and hockey, along with individual triumphs in wrestling, archery and golf, propelled India into the top five.The final tally of 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals ensured another top-five Asian Games finish and capped a campaign defined by historic firsts, successful title defences and a powerful finish.India may have fallen short of the Hangzhou record, but Aichi-Nagoya 2026 will be remembered as another landmark Asian Games campaign for Indian sport.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘I have only one life’: How 3 Idiots inspired Bobby Kumar's Asian Games journey
articles.summary: Kolkata: When Bihar’s Bobby Kumar watched the Bollywood blockbuster 3 Idiots, one message stayed with him: follow your passion.
articles.body: Kolkata: When Bihar’s Bobby Kumar watched the Bollywood blockbuster 3 Idiots, one message stayed with him: follow your passion.Growing up in a state where academics often take precedence over sport, Bobby found himself caught between expectations and his love for playing games. Inspired by the film’s message of pursuing what truly makes one happy, he chose a different path.Today, that decision has earned him an Asian Games bronze medal in sepak takraw as part of the Indian men’s quadrant team that reached the semifinals before losing to hosts Japan in Nagoya.“I have only one life. I didn’t want to spend it thinking only about studies,” Bobby recalled from Nagoya. “The message of 3 Idiots stayed with me. It made me feel that I should follow my heart and do what I truly enjoy.”Before discovering sepak takraw, Bobby played cricket in Patna. Like many families in Bihar, his parents, Manju Devi and Dharmendar Upadhyay, initially wanted him to focus on education and build a secure future. He tried, but sport proved impossible to ignore.“Whenever I saw other children playing, I wanted to play too. Gradually, I started enjoying it more and more and decided that I wanted to pursue sport seriously,” he said.It wasn’t cricket that eventually became his calling. Inspired by his elder brother Sunny, Bobby took up sepak takraw in 2014-15 and began training under coach Pankaj Kumar and Karunesh Kumar at a nearby park in Kankarbagh.“I could see his potential from the very beginning. He was disciplined, hardworking and eager to learn. That’s why I always believed he could achieve something special,” said Pankaj, who has been coaching since 2002.Bobby’s rise was steady and he completely committed himself to the sport in 2019 when he joined the Sports Authority of India (SAI) training centre in Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh.The road to the Asian Games, however, was far from smooth. Bobby was in contention for the previous edition but missed out after changes to the squad. Rather than letting the setback define him, he turned it into motivation.“I made the 2026 Asian Games my target. I wanted to make sure I was in the main squad and not just among the reserves,” he said. “I was so focused on that goal that I even included ‘2026’ in my passwords as a daily reminder.”That focus was tested by personal challenges. Yet, with support from teammates, particularly Akash Yumnam, Bobby managed to remain fully focused on the competition.India battled through a difficult group featuring powerhouses Myanmar and Vietnam before eventually securing bronze. For Bobby’s father, the medal was the reward for years of dedication.“I couldn’t be prouder of Bobby. He has always been passionate about sports. Even when he was studying at Kendriya Vidyalaya, he used to win medals in skipping events. Today, people recognise me because of what he has achieved. Everything he has earned has come through his hard work and commitment,” said Dharmendar, who also has a daughter named Isha Kumari.As for Pankaj, the achievement is equally satisfying.“Seeing him win an Asian Games medal is a matter of immense pride. As a coach, you always hope your students reach the biggest stage, and Bobby has done that,” he said.And if the coach’s assessment is accurate, the Asian Games bronze may only be the start. “Bihar is now among the strongest states in the country in this sport. We have several players competing at the national level, and Bobby’s medal will inspire many more youngsters to take it up,” Pankaj added.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Kumkum Mohod makes history with individual recurve gold, secures LA Olympics quota at Asian Games
articles.summary: OKAZAKI At the Asian Games, Kumkum Mohod has had very little to do with the world outside her competition.
articles.body: OKAZAKI At the Asian Games, Kumkum Mohod has had very little to do with the world outside her competition. She has stayed off social media, had limited access to her phone and used it mainly to communicate with her parents.On Friday, she sent a picture of her medals to her father, Anil. His response was immediate: “There is a medal missing in this photo.” Typical of Indian fathers, he was reminding her of the task at hand.Like an obidient daughter then, the 17-year-old from Maharashtra completed the picture. On Saturday at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium, she also wrote a slice of history that India — and South Korea — will remember for a long time. Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve archery gold at the Asian Games and, in the process, secured an Olympic quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Games.She finished her campaign with three medals: individual gold, women’s team gold and mixed team silver. Earlier, the trio of Ankita Bhakat, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum shattered South Korea’s dominance in the team event to claim their maiden gold.In the quarterfinals, Kumkum defeated Kang Chae-young 6-4. Kang, the 2025 individual world champion, was the favourite against an Indian prodigy who had qualified 10th. But Kumkum offered more than a glimpse of what was to come.In the semifinals, she swept aside China’s Jingyo Zhu 6-2.The final frontier was another Korean, Oh Ye-jin. And this time, Kumkum had to fight her way back.Oh took the opening set 29-27 and then moved 3-1 ahead. Kumkum responded with a perfect 30, only to follow it with consecutive 8s. Kumkum found her rhythm, produced a perfect 30 and forced the final into a shoot-off.One arrow now separated her from history. Oh shot an 8. Kumkum drew, aimed and released. A perfect 10.The shy 17-year-old had just done what no Indian recurve archer had done before at the Asian Games. A teenager who surprisingly enjoys listening to sad songs reserved those for the Koreans, for the Indians, she ensured there was only celebratory music.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India turn World Cup hurt into Asian Games gold, thrash Malaysia 5-1 to secure LA Olympics berth
articles.summary: KAKAMIGAHARA: After the World Cup debacle, plenty was on the line at the Asian Games — places in the team, jobs and, most importantly, an Olympic berth.
articles.body: KAKAMIGAHARA: After the World Cup debacle, plenty was on the line at the Asian Games — places in the team, jobs and, most importantly, an Olympic berth.If the semifinal win over Pakistan was a narrow escape, the Indian men’s hockey team responded to its critics in style on a nippy Saturday night, defending its gold for the first time.India came with a plan and, despite Malaysia’s razor-sharp counter-attacks and man-to-man defence, backed its skill with timing and precision to run out 5-1 winners at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium.It was one of the team’s most well-rounded performances in recent times.The occasion was special for Indian hockey. The men joined the women in securing qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics, completing a gold-medal double, another first for Indian hockey at the Asiad.The scoreline, however, did not tell the whole story. Malaysia were no pushovers. Both teams repeatedly took the aerial route to make inroads, though neither was able to establish sustained control.India broke the deadlock in the 11th minute when skipper Harmanpreet Singh’s low drag-flick rocketed past goalkeeper Zaimi Deris Mat. Malaysia responded almost immediately. Veteran Shello Silverius collected an aerial pass from Faiz Jali on top of the circle and found the left corner with a superb finish.The Indian goalkeepers, Suraj Karkera and HS Mohith, who had faced criticism for their performances, stood up when it mattered. Amid midfield errors at both ends and chaotic attacking exchanges, Jugraj Singh unleashed a powerful drag-flick in the 23rd minute to restore India’s lead.But a one-goal advantage is never enough, especially with two quarters still to play. At the break, India regrouped. The hurt and humiliation of the World Cup remained fresh, and the players were determined not to let their chance at redemption slip away.“I think it was one of the most important achievements we can ever have because of what happened in the World Cup. It was tough to handle physically but, more importantly, it was mentally exhausting. We had been working very hard for a very long time. The World Cup did not pan out the way we wanted, and we couldn’t allow this to slip away,” Hardik Singh said.India eventually pulled away in the third quarter. Awarded a penalty stroke for an infringement, they converted through Hardik in the 42nd minute.Shilanand Lakra, arguably India’s best player on the night, then scored from close range before Harmanpreet put the finishing touches on the victory with three minutes remaining. The celebrations were muted. Relief, more than euphoria, was the overriding emotion.“We played a great game. We almost needed that semifinal to get into this mindset. I’m proud of the guys because of the first half’s performance from Malaysia, they really did make it difficult for us,” said chief coach Craig Fulton.There have been long waits, titles defended and medals lost at these Games. But amid it all, Indian hockey has produced one of its most heartwarming stories. With the job done in Japan, the focus now shifts to the LA Olympics.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'If Rory can win the Masters, so can you': Pranavi Urs overcomes triple bogey to script historic Asian Games gold
articles.summary: Overnight leader Pranavi Urs was channelling her inner Rory McIlroy as she negotiated the unsettling bumps that came with the pressure of the final day in
articles.body: Overnight leader Pranavi Urs was channelling her inner Rory McIlroy as she negotiated the unsettling bumps that came with the pressure of the final day in the Asian Games women’s golf event.After she two-putted to golden glory on the rolling greens of Kasugai Country Club, she was a picture of calm, and quite unaware that she had sealed a historic first.Pranavi was in the zone. Only when playing partner Shannon Tan walked up to her, she realised her feat. “I thought it was to force a playoff,” she said. But it was the happy ending to an accomplished performance. It could also be a new beginning, instrumental in teeing off changes in the game back home.There was that gentle smile as she embraced her challengers. And then, she was ready for the customary soak by her friends Diksha Dagar and Aditi Ashok, with whom she shares team silver now. To go along with that shiny gold, thank you.“The first will always be the first. And I’ve always had that motto,” she said. “You are always going to have multiple winners, but you’re never going to have (another) first winner.”Last year, in a local ‘Battle of the Sexes’ battle on the IGPL circuit, the Mysuru golfer had emerged as the first woman to break through the barriers in a mixed field, beating boyfriend Karandeep Kochchar. “IGPL was good but gold beats it.”After playing in the howling wind and relentless rain on the Ayrshire links course of the Scottish Open, and leaving Las Vegas’ high-profile Aramco Championship with a creditable cut in a year she discovered new horizons, the 23-year-old Ladies European Tour (LET) golfer drew on all that mental fortitude in three sub-par rounds, and a fighting even-par final outing.With a three-stroke lead overnight, she admitted she and her anxious family, and boyfriend, couldn’t sleep in anticipation. “We all grew up in a joint family. Obviously, everyone couldn’t make it to Japan. My (cousin) sister Vidhatri, who also plays on the pro tour, was a nervous wreck. There’s always a live commentary going on in our group chats. And I told them, please record your reaction if I win. That was my last message before I teed off.”It was the Bollywood-style denouement her mother Kaivalya wanted. “It was always my mom’s dream to have me represent the country and win, and then the national anthem. I’m glad I could do it in front of my parents. Dad (Sharath) cried, probably for the second time in his life. It’s funny because he cried when I was born. I did it for them.”It didn’t come easy. After a 66-63-66 push on the par-70 course, Pranavi stumbled with a triple bogey on the 3rd before India saw the sun rise, and former Major champ and six-time LPGA winner Ruoning Yin became the woman to chase. For viewers back home, it felt like a reprise of the disappointment of Aditi missing out on a medal at the Tokyo Olympics.But this was never meant to be a case of the ‘yips’. Only ‘yippee’, as Pranavi invoked the spirit of Rory, who won his first elusive Masters in 2025, having conceded a ‘triple’ early on. “I was thinking, if he can go and win the Masters, so can you. And I made three birdies after that,” was her reply to the doubters.When World No. 6 Yin’s birdie putt lipped out on the 18th, Pranavi arrived for her date with destiny.Next is a sweet homecoming for Urs, as she hunts for another first — a Ladies European Tour title — at the Hero Women’s Indian Open a little more than a fortnight from now. There, she will re-acquaint herself with Tan, the defending champion.As Pranavi ended a 24-year wait for a golf gold, Busan 2002 gold medallist Shiv Kapur found himself applauding Pranavi’s efforts. “I woke up early to follow the competition and was struck by her ability to remain composed under pressure,” he said. “I lived every moment. I hope the medals will be a huge boost for the game in India.” he added.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 20 Hangzhou golds gone, 13 new routes to gold: How India’s Asian Games medal map changed
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India won 28 gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India won 28 gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Four years later, the question in Aichi-Nagoya was how many of those titles it could retain. The answer? - Eight, out of the 28 Hangzhou golds. That’s 28.6 per cent of the total. Twenty titles changed hands.The biggest changes came in the sports that had driven India's record campaign in Hangzhou. All seven shooting golds were lost, while all six athletics titles changed hands and, India also failed to retain either of its two individual compound archery golds.But just the gold-medal count does not tell the whole story. India retained the three compound team archery titles, both kabaddi golds, both cricket titles and the men's hockey crown.The other golds came from a different mix of events and athletes. Some had won silver or bronze in Hangzhou and moved up to gold in Japan. Others won titles in events where India had not been on the podium four years earlier.So while 20 of India's 28 Hangzhou champions failed to retain their titles, the gold medals themselves were replaced from a much wider pool. The Aichi-Nagoya campaign, in that sense, was less about defending the Hangzhou haul and more about how India's medal map had changed in four years.Shooting: from seven golds in Hangzhou to three in Aichi-NagoyaWhile Shooting had produced seven golds and 22 medals for India at Hangzhou, In Aichi-Nagoya, the overall medal tally fell to 15. The gold count dropped from seven to three, while silver moved from nine to eight and bronze from six to four. The biggest change was that none of India's seven Hangzhou golds was defended in the same event.Instead, India found gold elsewhere. Neeru Dhanda won the women's trap individual title and then partnered Kynan Chenai to win mixed trap. Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh added the mixed 10m air pistol gold.The rifle teams that had delivered two of India's Hangzhou golds - men's 10m air rifle and men's 50m rifle 3 Positions - returned with silver in Japan. There was also a new medal in mixed skeet. Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Parinaaz Dhaliwal won bronze, giving India its first Asian Games medal in the event.So while India's shooting haul was smaller in Aichi-Nagoya, the change was not just in the numbers. The seven golds from Hangzhou were gone, and the three titles in Japan came from a different set of events.Athletics: The medals stayed, the golds disappearedWhile India won 29 athletics medals in Hangzhou, Four years later, the tally in Aichi-Nagoya was 24. The bigger change, though, came in the gold count.Six golds in Hangzhou became one in Japan and that lone title came in the women's 4x400m relay, four years after India's men's relay team had won gold in Hangzhou. Silver medals fell from 14 to nine, while bronze medals increased from nine to 14.There was still plenty of continuity among India's medallists. Murali Sreeshankar again won silver in the long jump. Tajinderpal Singh Toor, the Hangzhou gold medallist, finished with silver this time. Tejaswin Shankar moved from silver to bronze in the decathlon, while Ancy Sojan retained her long-jump silver.Vithya Ramraj again won bronze in the 400m hurdles. Gulveer Singh improved on his Hangzhou performance in the 10,000m, moving from bronze to silver. He also added silver in the 1500m and bronze in the 5000m.So the athletics podium did not disappear in Aichi-Nagoya. India still won 23 medals outside gold. The difference was that performances that had produced six titles in Hangzhou produced only one gold four years later.Archery: The tally remains the same, but in different eventsIndia matched its Hangzhou tally in archery, winning nine medals again - five gold, two silver and two bronze. The medal distribution, however, changed considerably.The three compound team golds were retained and beyond those events, India had a different set of medal-winning performances in Aichi-Nagoya, particularly in the women's recurve events.Kumkum Mohod won individual recurve gold, while the women's recurve team moved from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Japan. That left the overall numbers unchanged, but the events behind those numbers were different.The individual compound events also saw a change. India had won medals in both the men's and women's individual compound events in Hangzhou. In Aichi-Nagoya, the men's individual compound event was the notable gap.Boxing: From no gold in Hangzhou to three in Aichi-NagoyaBoxing went in the opposite direction to shooting and athletics. India had returned from Hangzhou with four medals - one silver and three bronze - but no gold, but In Aichi-Nagoya, the haul rose to six, including three gold medals.Lovlina Borgohain upgraded her silver in the women's 75kg category in 2023, to gold four years later, while Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal added two more titles in categories where India had not won gold at Hangzhou. The bronze tally remained unchanged at three.Wrestling: Six medals again, but two golds this timeWrestling also finished with six medals, the same tally as Hangzhou. But the distribution changed completely. India had won one silver and five bronze medals in 2022, without a gold. In Aichi-Nagoya, that became two golds, two silvers and two bronze medals.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal supplied the two freestyle golds, while Nitesh, added a historic silver in Greco-Roman, and Antim Panghal upgraded her bronze from the 2022 Games to silver in 2026.The bronze tally fell from five to two (Sunil Kumar and Deepak Punia), but India added two golds and one silver.Squash: Five medals again, but both golds are goneSquash finished with five medals in both Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. But the two golds from 2022 were gone.India's tally changed from two gold, one silver and two bronze to two silver and three bronze. Abhay Singh retained the men's singles silver, replacing Saurav Ghosal on the podium. Anahat Singh added a women's singles medal.The men's team and mixed doubles titles from Hangzhou slipped to bronze in Japan. The women's team retained its bronze, while the mixed-team bronze was not repeated. The overall medal count stayed at five. The two golds did not.Kabaddi & Cricket: Four titles, no changeIndia had won all four golds available across the two sports in Hangzhou - the men's and women's cricket titles and the men's and women's kabaddi titles and it repeated that sweep in Japan.In the kabaddi double, both Indian teams came through against Iran in the finals, with the women winning 37-34 and the men 40-34. For the women's team, the victory extended an impressive Asian Games record. India has now won the women's kabaddi gold at every edition it has entered except the 2018 Jakarta Games, when Iran took the title and India settled for silver. The 2026 victory was therefore its fourth gold in five appearances.The men's side has an even longer record. India's 40-34 win over Iran was its ninth Asian Games gold in the men's event across 10 editions. The only time it failed to win the title was in 2018, when Iran took gold. India had returned to the top at Hangzhou and retained the crown in Nagoya.Cricket followed with its own repeat. India's women's team opened the 2026 Games by defending the title it had won at Hangzhou, beating Sri Lanka in the final. The men's team then completed the cricket double on October 3, beating Pakistan to retain the men's gold as well.Hockey: Men's gold defended, women's bronze turned into goldHockey produced two very different stories in Aichi-Nagoya. The men's gold was defended. The women's bronze became gold.For the men's team, the 2026 title was significant beyond the medal itself. India beat Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain the Asian Games crown for the first time, becoming only the second country after Pakistan to win consecutive men's hockey golds. The victory also secured direct qualification for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.The women's title was a different story altogether. India had finished with bronze in Hangzhou. In Japan, it beat defending champions China 1-0 to win the Asian Games gold for the first time since 1982. The victory ended a 44-year wait for gold and also secured direct qualification for LA 2028.It also produced a first for Indian hockey at the Asian Games. For the first time, both the men's and women's teams won gold at the same edition.Golf: A new gold, and a new first for Indian womenAt Hangzhou, Aditi Ashok won silver, giving India its first women's golf medal at the Asian Games. Four years later, Pranavi Urs went one better.She won individual gold, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf title. Urs then joined Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar to win India's first women's team medal in the sport. India's overall golf haul doubled from one medal in Hangzhou to two in Aichi-Nagoya.The individual gold also ended a 24-year wait for India. Shiv Kapur had won the men's title in 2002; Pranavi became the first Indian golfer since then to win an individual Asian Games gold.Sailing: Three medals again, but different eventsSailing produced the same number of medals in both editions. India won three medals in Hangzhou and three again in Aichi-Nagoya. But the events behind those medals changed.Two new skiff events produced podium finishes in Japan, replacing the men's windsurfer and men's dinghy medals from Hangzhou. The women's dinghy medal also changed colour, from silver to bronze.Badminton: Three medals became oneBadminton saw one of India's biggest drops between Hangzhou and Aichi-Nagoya. The medal tally fell from three to one. India's 2022 haul included Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty's men's doubles gold, the men's team silver and HS Prannoy's singles bronze.Four years later, the men's team remained India's only podium finisher. But even that medal changed colour, with the silver becoming bronze.Neither of the two individual medals from Hangzhou was defended. There was no individual podium finish in Aichi-Nagoya, leaving India with just one medal from a sport that had produced three in the previous edition.Rowing: Five medals fell to oneRowing's fall was even more pronounced. Five medals in Hangzhou became one bronze in Aichi-Nagoya. In 2022, India had taken two silver and three bronze medals across five events. In Japan, only Satnam Singh and Salman Khan's men's double sculls reached the podium.None of the five events that had delivered medals at Hangzhou did so again. And the build-up itself was unsettled, with last-minute changes to crew combinations and event entries. Arvind Singh, a 2022 silver medallist in the lightweight double sculls, was moved into the quadruple sculls, while Balraj Panwar shifted from the quadruple to the single sculls.Tennis: Two medals became none, and a 36-year streak endedTennis went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. The bigger change was the end of India's 36-year medal streak at the Asian Games.India had continued to find tennis medals across different generations, from Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi to Sania Mirza, Rohan Bopanna and the current doubles players. That run ended in Japan.India had three quarterfinal opportunities but could not convert any of them into a medal. Sumit Nagal went out in the singles quarterfinals, while India did not have a women's singles entry. The result was India's first medal-less Asian Games tennis campaign since 1986.Equestrian: Two medals became noneEquestrian went from two medals in Hangzhou to none in Aichi-Nagoya. India had won one gold and one bronze in 2022. There was no podium finish this time.The campaign was also affected by selection disputes, the absence of an approved show-jumping team and a setback in eventing. The result was a complete reversal from Hangzhou, with a two-medal haul turning into none in Japan.MMA and Soft Tennis: Two new entries on India's medal mapAichi-Nagoya also added two new sports to India's Asian Games medal list. Suchika Tariyal won bronze in the women's traditional MMA 60kg category, giving India its first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts.Jay Meena added another first in soft tennis, winning bronze in men's singles. For Meena, the medal came after two previous Asian Games appearances without a podium finish. He had competed at the 2018 and 2022 Games but returned without a medal on both occasions. In Nagoya, he finally reached the podium.Neither medal replaced a gold lost from Hangzhou. They came from sports that had not previously contributed an Asian Games medal to India.Weightlifting: 28 years later, Mirabai completes the collectionWeightlifting produced another long-gap story. Mirabai Chanu's silver in the women's 49kg category was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari's silver at Bangkok 1998.There was also a personal milestone. Chanu had Olympic and World Championship medals and Commonwealth Games titles, but an Asian Games medal had remained missing. The silver in Nagoya completed the collection.Kurash: Back on the podiumIndia had not won a kurash medal at the previous Asian Games. Pincky Balhara put the sport back on India's medal list in Aichi-Nagoya, winning bronze in the women's -78kg category. It was a return to the podium rather than a title defence, adding another sport to India's 2026 medal tally.Wushu, Table Tennis, sepak takraw: Medals from the wider fieldWushu again produced a medal through Roshibina Devi, who won silver in the women's 60kg sanda - her third Asian Games medal.Table tennis added bronze through Diya Chitale and Manush Shah in mixed doubles, while World No.3 men’s pair of Manush Shah and Manav Thakar flattered to deceive.India also retained its bronze in sepak takraw, with the men's quadrant team finishing on the podium again.The other side: Four sports drop out of India's medal listThe Hangzhou-to-Aichi-Nagoya comparison also has a different side. Some sports that had contributed medals in 2022 did not produce one in Japan.Chess, bridge, roller sports and canoeing had together contributed six medals to India's Hangzhou tally - two silver in chess, one silver in bridge, two bronze in roller sports and one bronze in canoeing. None of those four sports were part of the Aichi-Nagoya programme.Firsts for India at Asian Games 2026The changing medal map also showed up in the number of firsts India recorded in Aichi-Nagoya.Suchika Tariyal: Won India's first Asian Games medal in mixed martial arts, taking bronze in the women's traditional -60kg division.Jay Meena: Became India's first Asian Games medallist in soft tennis after reaching the semi-finals in men's singles.Neeru Dhanda: Won India's first individual gold medal of the Games in the women's trap event.Baranica Elangovan: Became the first Indian pole vaulter to win an Asian Games medal, taking bronze.Ankita Bhakat, Kumkum Mohod and Kirti Sharma: Won India's first women's team recurve gold at the Asian GamesKumkum Mohod: Became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games.Pranavi Urs: Became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games gold medal in golf.Sawan Barwal: Won India's first marathon medal since 1982, while setting a national record.Sarvesh Kushare: Ended India's 56-year wait for a high jump medal at the Asian Games.Anahat Singh: Became the first Indian to win a women's singles silver medal in squash at the Asian Games.Lovlina Borgohain: Became the second Indian woman boxer after Mary Kom to win Asian Games gold.India women's hockey team: Won the Asian Games title for the first time in 44 years.Mirabai Chanu: Won India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari's silver at Bangkok 1998.Seema Kumari: Ended a 16-year Indian medal drought in the women's 10,000m.Vithya Ramraj: Broke a 42-year-old national record in the women's 400m hurdles while winning bronze.The gold rush was not simply a repeatThirteen of India's 2026 gold medals came from events in which India had either won silver or bronze at Hangzhou, or had not won a medal at all. That included three shooting golds.The mixed 10m air pistol moved from silver to gold, while Neeru Dhanda won the women's individual trap and mixed trap titles in events where India had not won gold in Hangzhou.Athletics produced another upgrade, with the women's 4x400m relay moving from silver to gold.Archery's women's recurve team went from bronze to gold, while Kumkum Mohod added the individual recurve title.Boxing produced three more. Lovlina Borgohain moved from silver to gold in the women's 75kg category. Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal won titles in categories where India had not taken gold in Hangzhou.Wrestling followed the same pattern. Sujeet Kalkal won the men's 65kg title, while Aman Sehrawat moved from bronze in 2022 to gold in the 57kg category.In golf, Pranavi Urs turned Aditi Ashok's women's individual silver from Hangzhou into gold. Women's hockey completed another major upgrade, moving from bronze in Hangzhou to gold in Aichi-Nagoya.Taken together, these 13 golds explain why the 2026 campaign cannot be judged simply by counting how many Hangzhou champions retained their titles.India did lose 20 of its 28 Hangzhou golds, but several of those losses were replaced by athletes who had finished lower on the podium in 2022, or had not reached it at all.The fact that India defended only eight of its 28 Hangzhou golds does not mean the 2026 campaign simply replaced the previous one with a broader or better model. Hangzhou had a heavy concentration of gold at the top. Shooting won seven. Athletics won six. Archery won five. Together, those three disciplines accounted for 18 of India's 28 gold medals in 2022. That made Hangzhou's medal profile very different from Aichi-Nagoya.And the disciplines that lost the most golds in Japan did not disappear from the podium. Shooting remained one of India's biggest medal contributors with 15 medals. Athletics produced 24, while archery matched its Hangzhou total of nine. So the change was not that India's traditional strengths stopped producing medals. They simply produced fewer golds.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: The Price of a Title Shot: When challengers had to pay to face the champion
articles.summary: The upcoming world chess championship between defending champion D Gukesh of India and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will take place in
articles.body: The upcoming world chess championship between defending champion D Gukesh of India and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will take place in Geneva from November 22 to December 12. Organized under the aegis of FIDE, the match carries a prize fund of USD 2.5 million.The first world chess championship took place 140 years ago in the United States in 1886 between Wilhelm Steinitz (a Prague-born Austrian subject) and Johannes Zukertort (a British citizen). Played across three cities, the championship was contested for stakes totaling USD 4,000.What is interesting is how that USD 4,000 purse was assembled and how the match itself was organised. It was arranged under a private contract between the two contestants who had to agree to championship terms with each other. Each had to find backers willing to put USD 2,000 into the purse. Steinitz won by ten games to five, with five draws, in games played across New York, St. Louis and New Orleans.For its first six decades, the world championship was governed by bilateral contracts between the champion and the challenger, with the incumbent generally holding the stronger negotiating position. There was no fixed schedule. The champion decided whether to accept the challenge and on what conditions. The challenger had to find money from wealthy patrons or a club or another source.The system did not guarantee that the best player would have a shot at being the world champion.When the Best Player Could Not Buy His ShotAkiba Rubinstein is considered to be among the best players of the early 1900s. Born in Poland, Rubinstein was introverted and fanatical about chess. Rubinstein reached his peak around 1912, winning five consecutive tournaments that year (San Sebastián, Pistyan, Breslau, Warsaw and Vilna). When he challenged Emanuel Lasker (then champion) in 1912, Lasker agreed to play on the condition that Rubinstein raised the money. Lasker’s financial demands were high, and Rubinstein struggled to meet them.Eventually, plans were made for a match in the autumn of 1914. Sadly, the match never happened, as World War I broke out in 1914, denying Rubinstein his shot at the world title. Just before Rubinstein challenged Lasker, José Raúl Capablanca sent a letter of challenge to Lasker in November 1911.At this point, Lasker had already held the title for seventeen years. Lasker responded to Capablanca’s challenge with a list of seventeen conditions which sparked a bitter dispute between the two. Among other conditions that Capablanca deemed unfair, Lasker demanded that the challenger win by a margin of at least 2 games, or Lasker would keep the title.Lasker, Capablanca and a Battle Over ConditionsThe ensuing bitterness led to the two cutting off all communication. Negotiations resumed after the war, and the two signed an agreement in January 1920. However, in a dramatic twist in June 1920, Lasker resigned his world title in writing via a press announcement, declaring Capablanca his successor.Under a clause in their agreement, this made Capablanca champion, but the chess public was unwilling to accept a title handed over without a match. Lasker nevertheless agreed to play, while continuing to insist that Capablanca was already the champion. The world championship match finally happened in Havana, Cuba, in 1921 with a USD 20,000 purse, of which Lasker was guaranteed USD 11,000 and Capablanca USD 9,000 whatever the result. Capablanca dominated the contest and became the third World Chess Champion in 1921.Once champion, Capablanca proposed rules of his own in what came to be known as the London Rules. Under them, the champion could not be compelled to defend his title for a purse below USD 10,000. The champion received 20 percent as a fee, with the remaining 80 percent split 60:40 between the winner and the loser.This was a formidable sum in the 1920s. It took Alexander Alekhine almost five years to find financial support to challenge Capablanca. The Club Argentino de Ajedrez and Argentine supporters stepped in to put up the purse. This secured the official match in Buenos Aires, where Alekhine ultimately defeated Capablanca in 1927.How the Champion–Challenger System Hit Its LimitsIronically, the London Rules stood in the way of Capablanca’s return as a challenger. Alekhine insisted that a rematch would have to follow the same rules. Talks dragged on for years without result, for reasons historians still dispute, and Capablanca died in 1942 without getting another shot at the title.This system of bilateral challenges ended in 1946 with the death of Alekhine. Alekhine still held the title at his death. There was nobody to challenge or negotiate with. FIDE, founded in 1924, stepped in.The Soviet Union joined FIDE in 1947, and in 1948 FIDE organised a world championship tournament. Five leading players took part, with Mikhail Botvinnik emerging as the winner and the new world champion. The subsequent qualifying cycle and tournaments were held under the aegis of FIDE with FIDE setting the rules.FIDE retained elements of the old structure. The champion still does not need to qualify and gets to defend the title. The challenger is determined through the cycle.Chess was hardly unique in using the champion–challenger model. Real tennis, the indoor game from which lawn tennis descends, claims the oldest world championship in any sport. Its first recorded champion, a Frenchman known only as Clergé, held the title in the 1740s, and it has always been decided by challenge. For long periods, the champion could accept or refuse a challenger, usually according to how much prize money the challenger’s sponsor offered, and several years could pass between matches.Professional boxing retained the champion–challenger structure but added sanctioning bodies to police it. A champion must periodically face a designated mandatory challenger or give up the belt. If the two camps cannot agree on terms, the sanctioning body holds a purse bid: promoters submit sealed offers, and the highest bidder stages the fight.Today, Sindarov does not have to find wealthy patrons or negotiate with Gukesh. He has already earned his seat across the board through a qualifying system. That may be the greatest difference between Geneva in 2026 and New York in 1886. The prize money has risen from thousands to millions, but the real progress is that a challenger no longer has to buy a shot at the title.(Aarav Dengla is India’s 93rd Grandmaster. He is a keen observer and student of world history in general and chess history in particular.)Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: West Indies beat India in record chase as Hope hits 162 in third ODI
articles.summary: Shai Hope’s 162 leads the West Indies to a record cricket run chase as they beat India by five wickets in the third ODI.
articles.body:
Captain Shai Hope’s unbeaten 162 led West Indies to a record run-chase win against India in one-day international cricket in Chandigarh.

The West Indies achieved their highest ODI run chase on Saturday, reaching 352-5 and winning by five wickets with 10 balls to spare after India made 351-7, featuring Lokesh Rahul’s 129 not out.

India had already won the three-match series after eight-wicket wins in Thiruvananthapuram and Guwahati. But the West Indies, chasing for the first time in the series, overcame India for the first time since 2023.

Hope promoted himself to opening batter after Jewel Andrew reportedly injured a finger making a catch and had to go to hospital. After keeping wicket for all of India’s 50 overs in high humidity, he batted brilliantly to score his second successive hundred in the series but struggled in the last overs.

“Felt something around the groin area but wanted to fight through till the end,” Hope said.

His second-highest ODI score, from 143 balls, included 17 boundaries and three sixes. Amir Jangoo added 67 off 56 and Keemo Paul 44 off 35.

“[Chasing is] always a lot easier in India, especially with the dew,” Hope said. “Glad we got over the line.”

Hope and Jangoo added 109 off 99 balls for the second wicket to defy an India bowling attack that recalled Mohammed Siraj and all-rounder Nitish Reddy and included debutant pacer Anshul Kamboj, who went wicketless.

Jangoo was run out in the 21st over, but Sherfane Rutherford (24) did not let the momentum slip. He added 56 with Hope, who reached 50 off 46 balls and 100 off 104 in his 21st ODI hundred and fifth against India.

Paul’s cameo included five fours as he added 65 off 61 balls with his skipper. Hope shifted gears after Paul was dismissed in the 41st over, caught off Gurnoor Brar.

Hope hit seven more fours and two sixes after his milestone, taking 62 off the last 39 balls faced to rush West Indies to victory.

India had to serve a slow over rate penalty for the last four overs, with an additional fielder inside the 30-yard circle, as Hope and Gudakesh Motie (19 not out) added 62 off 29 balls for the sixth wicket.

India won the toss again but skipper Shubman Gill was caught behind on 1 and Virat Kohli was bowled for a golden duck. Both fell to Jayden Seales.

Only 28 runs came in the first 10 overs, then Rohit Sharma and Rahul propelled the hosts.

Sharma resurrected the innings with 92 off 85 balls, adding 137 for the third wicket with Ruturaj Gaikwad.

Sharma took his time and was unlucky to miss a second consecutive hundred in the series; he was caught off Paul in the 25th over.

Four overs later, Gaikwad — 57 off 69 — was Seales’s third wicket.

That brought Rahul to the crease, and he led the charge past 350.

Rahul hit six sixes and 10 fours. He scored 50 off 41 balls and his second 50 off 39 balls. He enjoyed good partnerships with Naman Dhir and Brar and finished 129 not out off only 87 balls.

The teams begin a five-match Twenty20 series on Tuesday, starting in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.
